headline: Kyōwa is from Middle Chinese 共和, and Mitsukuri Shōgo later used it for the United States.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 共和 (gjowngH hwa).

The idea of "government without a king" was later adopted by Japanese geographer Mitsukuri Shōgo in reference to the United States, which he dubbed 共和政治州 (Kyōwa-Seiji-Shū, literally “the States with Cooperative and Harmonious Government”); Mitsukuri anecdotally took this suggestion from a Ruist acquaintance who could only think of the aforementioned regency as the sole example of an East Asian government with no monarch. Later Japanese authors used 共和 in a rather indiscriminate way, for anything from commonwealth, to republic, to democracy. The original translation into Chinese of English republican was Chinese 民主 (mínzhǔ), whence Vietnamese dân chủ (“democracy”).

headline: Jari may be a shift from the sazare of 細石 (sazareishi, “gravel, pebble”), but jari is cited to 1619 and zari only to 1677.

sources.quote: Listed in one source as possibly a shift from the sazare portion of 細石 (sazareishi, “gravel, pebble”, literally “small + stone”).
* /sazare/ → */zare/ → /zari/ → /d͡ʑari/
However, the first attestation of the zari form is not until 1677, while the jari form is first cited to 1619.
The child sense originates as a jargon term at places such as a theatre, initially in reference to child visitors.

headline: Uwaki is 上 (uwa, “over”) plus 気 (ki, “spirit”), with 浮 an example of jukujikun.

sources.quote: /ufa ki/ → /uwaki/
Compound of 上(うわ) (uwa, “over”) + 気(き) (ki, “spirit”). The use of 浮 is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

headline: Kokoroe is the continuative stem of the verb 心得る (kokoroeru, “to know, understand”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 心(こころ)得(え)る (kokoroeru, “to know, understand”), from classical verb 心(こころ)得(う) (kokorou, see below).

headline: Ninshiki is a compound 認識, literally “know, recognize; know, remember”, which the source compares to Mandarin rènshi.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese compound 認識 /认识 (nyinᴴ syik, literally “know, recognize; know, remember”). Compare modern Mandarin rènshi, Eastern Min nêng-sék.

headline: Tobira is 戸 (to, “door”) plus 片 (hira, “broad, flat thing”), with hira voiced to bira by rendaku.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 戸 (to, “door”) + 片 (hira, “broad, flat thing”). The hira shifted to bira in Middle Japanese, an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Fudōsan was coined by Mitsukuri Rinsho as a translation of French immobilier.

sources.quote: Coined by Mitsukuri Rinsho as a translation of French immobilier.

meaning: to be ruined, to perish, to be destroyed
headline: Horobiru is a shift from the Classical Japanese verb 滅ぶ (horobu).

sources.quote: From Classical Japanese verb 滅(ほろ)ぶ (horobu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

headline: Chūsen is 抽 (chū, “to draw, to pull out”) plus 籤 (sen, “lots”), with 選 a daiyōji replacing 籤.

sources.quote: Sino-Japanese compound of 抽(ちゅう) (chū, “to draw, to pull out”) + 籤(せん) (sen, “lots”). 選 is a daiyōji replacing 籤.

headline: Bunsho is from the Middle Chinese compound 文書, in the kan'on reading, now the most common one.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 文書 (*miən *shiu). Compare modern Chinese 文書 /文书 (wénshū).
The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Now the most common reading for this term.

headline: Kusa, “grass”, is from Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kusa, and is found in the Man'yōshū.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kusa. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE. Possibly cognate with Korean 꽃 (kkot, “flower”).
The development of the fake, amateur senses is unclear, but probably from an earlier meaning green, referring to the color of the grass.
From the resemblance of multiple repetitions of w (w, “LOL”) to grass: wwwwwwwww.
Possibly influenced by the term くすくす (kusukusu), an adverb indicating stifled laughter.
